title: AI for Executives, Leaders, and Decision Makers
summary: This intermediate module enables leaders to evaluate proposed AI uses, assign decision rights, demand decision-relevant evidence, and establish monitoring and escalation rules. After completing it, learners can turn an AI proposal into a documented decision to proceed, revise, restrict, pause, or reject.
objectives: Classify an AI proposal by organizational impact, uncertainty, reversibility, and exposure.
Define accountable owners and decision rights for an AI use.
Request evidence that connects system performance to a specific organizational outcome and operating context.
Write approval conditions, monitoring measures, escalation thresholds, and stop conditions.
Distinguish responsibility that can be assigned to a provider from accountability that remains with the adopting organization.
Make and document a decision to proceed, revise, restrict, pause, or reject an AI proposal.

sections.title: Level and Scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes familiarity with ordinary organizational planning, budgeting, risk, and accountability, plus a basic understanding that AI systems produce outputs from data and instructions. It does not assume programming, model-building, statistical, or procurement expertise.

The executive task is not to determine whether AI is impressive in the abstract. It is to decide whether a defined use should be authorized under defined conditions. A complete decision identifies the intended outcome, affected people, accountable owner, supporting evidence, permitted boundaries, monitoring measures, and conditions for escalation or stopping.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology organizes AI risk work around four functions: Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Govern is cross-cutting, while the other functions address context, assessment, prioritization, and response. This module converts those functions into a practical leadership sequence rather than a technical implementation procedure.
sections.callout: Do not approve a general capability. Approve or reject a specific use, in a specific context, with a named owner and explicit conditions.

sections.title: Define the Decision Before Reviewing the Technology
paragraphs: Begin with a one-sentence decision statement: the organization is considering using an AI-enabled process to support a named task for named users in a named setting. State whether the output advises a person, prioritizes work, generates content, or directly triggers an action. This boundary prevents evidence about one use from being treated as proof for a different use.

Next, define the intended organizational outcome without referring to the AI itself. Examples include reducing unresolved requests, helping employees locate approved information, or improving the consistency of a review process. Then identify the present baseline. Without a baseline, a later change cannot be interpreted as improvement, deterioration, or no meaningful change.

Separate the output from the outcome. Producing a response is an output. Resolving a request correctly is an outcome. Classifying a case is an output. Making a timely and appropriate decision is an outcome. Executive evidence should connect output quality to the outcome that justified the proposal.

Identify who is affected, who operates the process, who can challenge an outcome, who can authorize changes, and who remains accountable. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development principles emphasize human rights, transparency, robustness, safety, and accountability. Those concerns require attention to people and operating context, not only to technical performance.

sections.title: Triage by Impact, Uncertainty, Reversibility, and Exposure
paragraphs: A practical portfolio triage uses four questions. Impact asks how serious a wrong or delayed outcome could be. Uncertainty asks how much relevant evidence is missing or how different the intended setting is from the tested setting. Reversibility asks whether an affected person and the organization can detect and correct an error. Exposure asks how many people, decisions, records, or business processes could be affected.

These dimensions guide the strength of review rather than producing an automatic score. A low-impact, reversible use with bounded exposure may justify a limited trial. A use with serious possible consequences, weak evidence, difficult correction, or broad exposure requires stronger review and controls. If the organization cannot describe the consequences or affected population, uncertainty remains unresolved and should not be silently treated as low risk.

Triage must consider the complete process. Human review does not by itself make a use safe or accountable. Leaders should ask whether reviewers have enough time, information, authority, and skill to detect and correct a problematic output. If they are expected merely to confirm it, the review control has not been demonstrated.

Record the reasoning behind the classification. The record should explain which consequences matter, what evidence is absent, how an error can be corrected, and what limits exposure. This allows a later reviewer to understand the decision instead of reconstructing it from memory.
sections.callout: High uncertainty is not evidence of high or low performance. It means the evidence is insufficient for the proposed decision.

sections.title: Assign Governance and Decision Rights
paragraphs: Name one accountable business owner for the use. That owner is responsible for the organizational outcome and for ensuring that approval conditions remain satisfied. Other roles may operate the process, assess evidence, protect information, review legal obligations, or respond to incidents, but distributing tasks does not eliminate the need for accountable ownership.

Define decision rights before deployment. Specify who may approve initial use, change its scope, accept a known limitation, pause operation, restore operation, and retire the use. Also specify who can receive and investigate challenges from affected people. Ambiguous decision rights delay action when conditions change.

Responsibility for supporting work may be assigned to an external provider, but the adopting organization still needs its own decision about the use. Provider evidence can inform that decision, yet it does not establish that the system is appropriate in every local workflow, population, or consequence setting.

The Govern function in the National Institute of Standards and Technology framework is cross-cutting. For leaders, this means accountability, policy, roles, risk tolerance, and oversight should shape mapping, measurement, and management rather than appearing only at the final approval meeting.

sections.title: Demand Decision-Relevant Evidence
paragraphs: Ask first what claim the evidence is meant to support. A useful claim names the task, population, operating conditions, outcome measure, and acceptable boundary. Evidence from a different task or setting may be informative, but its relevance must be explained rather than assumed.

Review evidence in four categories. Outcome evidence addresses whether the process achieves the intended result. Risk evidence addresses errors, harmful effects, security, privacy, and unequal effects on relevant groups. Operational evidence addresses whether people can use, supervise, challenge, and recover from the process. Economic evidence addresses the full organizational resources required to operate, review, correct, monitor, and retire the use.

For every measure, request a baseline, a decision threshold, a measurement method, a measurement frequency, an owner, and a predefined response. A measure without a threshold cannot by itself determine whether action is required. A threshold without an owner and response does not create an operating control.

Ask how testing represents the intended setting. Relevant questions include whether test cases cover ordinary and difficult conditions, whether affected groups are represented, whether reviewers used the same information and time constraints expected in operation, and whether failures were examined rather than averaged away.

Do not convert missing evidence into an unsupported claim. Record the item as UNKNOWN, identify what observation or test would establish it, and decide whether the unresolved uncertainty permits a bounded trial, requires more evidence, or prevents the proposed use.

sections.title: Set Boundaries, Controls, and Human Recourse
paragraphs: Approval conditions should state where the use is permitted and prohibited. Boundaries can cover eligible tasks, users, information, affected populations, output types, and actions that require independent authorization. A narrow boundary makes both evidence and accountability more specific.

Controls should address prevention, detection, response, and recovery. Prevention reduces the chance of an unacceptable event. Detection identifies when performance or operating conditions depart from expectations. Response assigns immediate action and communication. Recovery restores an acceptable process, corrects affected records or decisions where possible, and captures lessons for future decisions.

Provide a workable route for questions and challenges when people may be affected. The route should identify where a challenge goes, who reviews it, what information is available to the reviewer, and who can correct an outcome. Merely stating that a person remains involved does not establish meaningful recourse.

Document exceptions. If leaders accept a limitation, the record should state the reason, scope, duration, compensating control, accountable approver, and review date. An exception without an end or review condition can become an undocumented permanent policy.

sections.title: Choose and Document a Decision
paragraphs: A leadership decision can be to proceed, revise, restrict, pause, or reject. Proceed means the evidence and controls support the defined use. Revise means the proposal needs changes before authorization. Restrict means only a narrower use or population is authorized. Pause means a temporary stop is required while specified evidence or remediation is completed. Reject means the proposed use is not acceptable under the considered conditions.

The decision record should contain the use statement, intended outcome, baseline, affected parties, impact and uncertainty assessment, evidence reviewed, unresolved UNKNOWN items, accountable owner, decision rights, boundaries, controls, measures, thresholds, escalation path, stop conditions, review date, and final rationale.

A decision record should distinguish facts from judgments. Test results, incident records, and observed process measures are evidence. Risk tolerance and acceptance of a tradeoff are governance judgments. Both belong in the record, but presenting a judgment as if it were measured evidence prevents meaningful review.

Approval is not the end of governance. It is permission to operate while stated assumptions and conditions remain valid. A material change in purpose, population, workflow, information, consequences, or observed performance requires reassessment because the original evidence may no longer answer the same question.
sections.callout: An approval without boundaries, monitoring, and stop conditions is incomplete.

sections.title: Monitor Outcomes and Trigger Action
paragraphs: Monitoring should cover the intended outcome, known failure modes, operational behavior, challenges from affected people, incidents, corrective actions, and changes in context. Select measures because they inform a decision, not because they are easy to collect.

Each measure needs an action rule. A rule states what condition triggers investigation, restriction, pause, correction, or executive review. The threshold may be quantitative or qualitative, but it must be defined before the organization needs to rely on it.

Stop conditions identify circumstances in which continued operation is not authorized. Examples include loss of an essential control, evidence of a serious unaddressed effect, operation outside the approved boundary, inability to provide required review, or failure to produce required monitoring evidence. The accountable owner must know who can activate the stop and what process replaces the AI-enabled step.

Review dates are useful, but event-based review is also necessary. Reassessment should occur when the purpose, affected population, workflow, consequences, evidence, or operating environment changes materially. The decision record should state which changes count as review triggers.

After completing this module, a learner can take a proposal that previously consisted mainly of a capability description and convert it into an outcome-focused decision record with ownership, evidence requirements, boundaries, monitoring rules, escalation paths, and stop conditions.

questions.prompt: What should a leader define before deciding whether evidence supports an AI proposal?
choices: The broad capability that appears most impressive
The specific use, intended outcome, affected people, and operating context
A permanent approval date
A provider's preferred demonstration
questions.explanation: The module requires leaders to define a specific use, outcome, affected parties, and context before judging evidence. Evidence cannot be evaluated for relevance when the decision boundary is undefined.

questions.prompt: A proposed use has potentially serious consequences, limited relevant evidence, and errors that would be difficult to correct. Which response best follows the module's triage method?
choices: Treat it as low risk because no failure has yet been observed
Approve it because a person will be present somewhere in the process
Require stronger review and controls, and do not treat missing evidence as low risk
Ignore reversibility because only measured performance matters
questions.explanation: Serious impact, high uncertainty, and difficult reversibility require stronger review and controls. Missing evidence remains uncertainty and does not prove safety or performance.

questions.prompt: Which set of elements makes a monitoring measure usable as an operating control?
choices: A measure name and a presentation date
A favorable example and a general promise to review it
A baseline, threshold, method, frequency, owner, and predefined response
A provider description without a local outcome
questions.explanation: The module states that every measure needs a baseline, decision threshold, method, frequency, owner, and response. Together these elements connect observation to accountable action.

questions.prompt: What happens to organizational accountability when supporting work is assigned to an external provider?
choices: The adopting organization no longer needs an accountable owner
Accountability automatically transfers to the provider
The organization still needs its own accountable owner and decision about the use
Only the provider may pause the use
questions.explanation: Provider evidence and services can support a decision, but the adopting organization remains responsible for deciding whether the specific use is appropriate in its own context.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a stop condition?
choices: A circumstance in which continued operation is no longer authorized
A target that is reviewed only after retirement
A general preference for future improvement
A substitute for naming an accountable owner
questions.explanation: A stop condition defines when operation must cease, such as loss of an essential control or operation outside the approved boundary. It must be connected to authority and a replacement process.
